---
title: "Coding a categorical predictor"
---

The [design-matrix page](design-matrices.qmd) used numeric predictor columns. A categorical predictor must first be represented by numeric columns whose row patterns determine the coefficient comparisons.

Suppose a verb-type predictor has three levels:

$$
\{\text{result},\text{manner},\text{stative}\}.
$$

A regression equation needs numerical columns. A [**contrast coding**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) turns the levels into columns whose coefficients represent declared comparisons.

The categories themselves have no numerical distance. We cannot subtract
*manner* from *stative* in the way we subtract two frequency values. The coding
supplies numeric rows that make particular comparisons estimable.

## Choose a reference level

Use result verbs as the reference and create two indicator columns:

| verb type | manner column $M$ | stative column $S$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| result | 0 | 0 |
| manner | 1 | 0 |
| stative | 0 | 1 |

The linear predictor is

$$
\eta
=\beta_0+\beta_M M+\beta_S S.
$$

## Substitute each row

For a result verb, both indicators are zero:

$$
\eta_{\text{result}}=\beta_0.
$$

For a manner verb,

$$
\eta_{\text{manner}}=\beta_0+\beta_M.
$$

For a stative verb,

$$
\eta_{\text{stative}}=\beta_0+\beta_S.
$$

Thus $\beta_M$ is the manner-minus-result difference on the linear-predictor scale, and $\beta_S$ is the stative-minus-result difference.

The intercept is the result-verb mean because the result row contains zeros in
both contrast columns. The two slope coefficients each compare another category
with that same reference.

## Reconstruct coefficients from category means

Suppose the fitted mean ratings are

| verb type | fitted mean |
|---|---:|
| result | 5.8 |
| manner | 5.2 |
| stative | 6.1 |

Under the displayed reference coding,

$$
\beta_0=5.8.
$$

The manner coefficient is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_M
&=\eta_{\text{manner}}-\eta_{\text{result}}\\
&=5.2-5.8\\
&=-.6.
\end{aligned}
$$

The stative coefficient is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_S
&=\eta_{\text{stative}}-\eta_{\text{result}}\\
&=6.1-5.8\\
&=.3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these coefficients recovers all three means:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\text{result}}&=5.8,\\
\eta_{\text{manner}}&=5.8-.6=5.2,\\
\eta_{\text{stative}}&=5.8+.3=6.1.
\end{aligned}
$$

This reconstruction is the safest check on a contrast interpretation.

## Set the reference in R

```{r}
#| label: set-reference-category
#| echo: true
cloze <- data.frame(
  verb_type = c("result", "manner", "stative")
)

cloze$verb_type <- relevel(
  factor(cloze$verb_type),
  ref = "result"
)

model.matrix(~ verb_type, data = cloze)
```

Software otherwise may choose a reference alphabetically. That default can make the coefficient table answer a comparison different from the theoretical question.

The column names printed by `model.matrix()` identify the represented
comparisons. The order of rows follows the observations, while factor level
order determines the reference and the contrast columns.

## Why use only two columns?

With an intercept and three unrestricted indicators, the three indicators sum to the intercept column of ones. This exact dependency prevents unique coefficient estimates.

Two columns suffice to represent three group locations relative to a reference.

More specifically, the intercept supplies the result location. The manner
column supplies the change needed to reach the manner location, and the stative
column supplies the change needed to reach the stative location. A third
indicator would duplicate information already present in the intercept and two
contrasts.

## Coding changes coefficients, not fitted group means

If we make manner the reference, the intercept and comparison coefficients change. The model can still produce the same fitted value for result, manner, and stative verbs.

For the three means above, making manner the reference yields

$$
\beta_0^*=5.2,
$$

$$
\beta_R^*=5.8-5.2=.6,
$$

and

$$
\beta_S^*=6.1-5.2=.9.
$$

The numbers differ from the result-reference coefficients, but the category
means remain 5.8, 5.2, and 6.1. Coding changes the coordinate system used to
describe the same fitted values.

Choose coding to make the theoretically relevant comparison direct. If the hypothesis concerns manner versus result, treatment coding with one of those levels as reference makes the coefficient immediately readable.

The stative-minus-manner comparison is not a single displayed coefficient under
result reference coding. It is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\text{stative}}-\eta_{\text{manner}}
&=(\beta_0+\beta_S)-(\beta_0+\beta_M)\\
&=\beta_S-\beta_M.
\end{aligned}
$$

With the example values, this difference is $.3-(-.6)=.9$. The comparison is
fully represented even though it does not appear in one coefficient row.

The displayed coefficient rows are not the only available comparisons. Predictions and linear
combinations can recover any comparison represented by the fitted category
means.

::: {.callout-note title="Check one comparison"}
1. Using the table above, express the stative-minus-manner difference in terms
   of $\beta_S$ and $\beta_M$.
2. Reconstruct the three fitted means from $\beta_0=5.8$,
   $\beta_M=-.6$, and $\beta_S=.3$.
3. Why do three category means require only an intercept and two contrast
   columns?
4. Explain why the displayed coefficient rows are not the only comparisons available from the fitted model.
:::
